catalog_quote: Stress in Ibanag is phonemic. A change in stress signals a change in meaning. Examples: agal ("call"); agál ("liver); pitu ("whistle"); pitú ("seven"); anâ ("son, daughter"); anà ("offspring, children"). Intonation and rhythm depend upon the unstressed and stressed syllables of speech. In an utterance, important words are stressed with one primary stress occurring in the utterance. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered p.505 (PDF page 5) of to an image and read it. Under the heading 'Prosodic Features' the text reads exactly: 'Stress in Ibanag is phonemic. A change in stress signals a change in meaning. Examples: agal ("call"); agál ("liver); pitu ("whistle"); pitú ("seven"); anâ ("son, daughter"); anà ("offspring, children"). Intonation and rhythm depend upon the unstressed and stressed syllables of speech. In an utterance, important words are stressed with one primary stress occurring in the utterance.' -- verbatim as reported (the PDF's OmniPage text layer garbles anâ/anà as 'anti'/'and', but the page image matches the report). p.502 'Proposal for Change' also confirmed on the ima…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive between the penultimate and the final syllable (agal vs agál, pitu vs pitú, bátu 'stone'.. etc.); it is not fixed by position. Corroborated first-hand by Peace Corps/Pascasio 1968 p.3 ('Stress is phonemic.. /batu/ cue ball vs /batú/ stone'; primary stress 'most frequently occurs on the final syllable'; stressed vowels longer and higher-pitched), by Brandes & Scheerer 1927 p.10 (ultima stress marked with acute, otherwise 'the weight of the voice falls, thru duration, on the penult'), and by Ibarbia 1969 p.x (one prominent syllable per word, 'generally the penultimate or the final'). Cuevas 1854 and Bauza 1996 add that accent shift alone can mark plural (Abbíng > Ábbing; anâ > anà).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None of the sources describes secondary stress; Peace Corps 1968 notes a post-tonic syllable may carry higher pitch than the stressed syllable when two or more syllables follow the stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sources disagree on which position is the unmarked/more frequent one: Brandes & Scheerer 1927 treat penult (realised as vowel duration) as the default and mark only ultima stress; Peace Corps 1968 says primary stress most frequently falls on the final syllable and marks only non-final stress; Ibarbia 1969 says stress 'shifts' in context and 'does not seem to be as important in Ibanag as it is in English'. Accent shift to the first syllable forms plurals of some kin terms (Cuevas 1854 num.53, 56; Bauza 1996 p.502) and emphatic superlatives (Cuevas num.119).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word in citation form (dictionary headwords, minimal pairs); Bauza and Ibarbia separately note one primary stress per utterance/phrase in connected speech. Variety: Tuguegarao (Central) Ibanag for Peace Corps 1968 and Bauza 1996; Brandes & Scheerer's speaker also Tuguegarao.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Ibanag proper (iban1267), mostly the Tuguegarao (Central/'standard') variety: Peace Corps 1968 and Bauza 1996 are based on Tuguegarao speech (speaker H. G. Bauza), Brandes & Scheerer 1927's informant likewise Tuguegarao; Verstraelen's text is from Pamplona (Northern Ibanag). No separate glottocodes for these dialects.

sources.note: p.3 (bundle p.21): 'Stress. Stress is phonemic. Thus the position of the stress distinguishes /batu/ 'cue ball' from /batú/ 'stone.' Stressed vowels are usually longer than unstressed vowels and also higher in pitch. However, if two or more syllables follow a stress, the syllable immediately following the stress has a higher pitch..' and 'Primary stress, which most frequently occurs on the final syllable, is not marked in that position. When it occurs elsewhere, it is written with an acute accent.' Verified on page image (scanned of image-only PDF).

sources.note: Libro I cap. I-II (letters, vowels, diphthongs, geminates) has no general accent rule; words carry acute accents on penult or final (Babáy, Baláy, Danúm vs Bábbay, Bábbal); num.53 and 56: certain kin nouns form the plural 'con solo mudarles el acento a la primera sílaba' (Abbíng > Ábbing; Babáy > Bábbay); num.119: superlatives by accent shift with lengthening. Implies contrastive, morphologically exploitable accent.
